title: Typography
summary: Starter decisions for type. Schemes are described, not computed.

questions.prompt: Which font family group do you use?
questions.summary: A group, not a licensed font file.

options.label: System sans
options.why: A system sans font loads fast and matches the device.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you do not ship a custom font yet.

options.label: System serif
options.why: A system serif can make long text feel like a document.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if long reading is the main job.

options.label: System mono
options.why: A mono font suits code and data that must align.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the product is mostly code or figures.
trade_offs: Long prose is harder to read.

questions.prompt: Which type scale ratio do you use?
questions.summary: The ratio is a named scheme.

options.label: 1.125 major second
options.why: A 1.125 ratio keeps heading steps close to body text.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if headings should stay quiet.
trade_offs: Hierarchy can be hard to see.
options.formula: Multiply the base size by 1.125 each step.

options.label: 1.2 minor third
options.why: A 1.2 ratio gives headings a clear step without a huge jump.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if headings should be obvious but not huge.
options.formula: Multiply the base size by 1.2 each step.

options.label: 1.25 major third
options.why: A 1.25 ratio is a major third. Steps are clear and not huge.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you want obvious heading steps.
trade_offs: Small screens may need fewer steps.
options.formula: Multiply the base size by 1.25 each step.

options.label: 1.333 perfect fourth
options.why: A perfect fourth makes display type much larger than body text.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if you need a strong display size.
trade_offs: You may not need every step.
options.formula: Multiply the base size by 1.333 each step.

questions.prompt: What is the base font size?
questions.summary: The size of body text before the ratio is applied.

options.why: Fourteen pixels suits dense tools and tight labels.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if the product is a dense tool.

options.why: Sixteen pixels is the common browser default for body text.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if body text should match the browser default.
trade_offs: Dense tools often want smaller text.

options.why: Eighteen pixels gives body text more presence.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if readers need a larger body size.
trade_offs: Fewer words fit on a line.

questions.prompt: What line height do you use for body text?
questions.summary: Line height is a ratio, not a calculated layout.

options.label: 1.3 tight
options.why: A tight line height keeps labels compact.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if most text is short labels.

options.label: 1.5 normal
options.why: A line height of 1.5 gives body text room without looking loose.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if body copy is the main content.
trade_offs: Tight UI labels can look tall.

options.label: 1.7 loose
options.why: A loose line height gives long text more air.
options.when_to_choose: Choose this if people read long passages.

questions.summary: References the global unit. Type does not copy the options.
